lead: Malthus: 1798 Essay (Gutenberg 4239) vs 2nd/later editions ('I have so far differed in principle from the former')
reason: Announcement is real (Preface to the 2nd ed., June 1803, reprinted in every later edition) but the later text is only available as a poor OCR (archive.org 1890 reprint of the 6th ed.) that garbles the key sentence ('does not ccme under the head either of vice or misery'); the 1806/1809/1817 OCR prints use long-s or lack the preface. Also early and later are editions of one titled work, which breaks the 'different works' rule even though Malthus himself says the 1803 Essay 'may be considered as a new work'.

lead: Ricardo: 'On Machinery' (ch. 31, Principles 3rd ed. 1821) vs an earlier separate work
reason: Gutenberg #33310 is the 1817 first edition and has no chapter 31; the only early praise-of-machinery evidence found is an editor's remark in the Letters to Malthus (#36345), not Ricardo's own early statement in a separate work.

lead: Brownson: The Laboring Classes (1840) vs The Convert (1857)
reason: The Convert quotes the 1840 essay at length and defends it ('place me where I stood then ... I would to-day repeat, and endorse every paragraph'); it does not retract the essay's thesis, and early text would be inside the later work. No clean announced passage.

lead: Spencer: Social Statics (1851) on land vs Justice (1891)
reason: Searched the archive.org OCR of Justice (1891) for a retraction of the 'right to the use of the Earth' chapter (grep for formerly/abandon/Social Statics); found only a general note that the book differs from Social Statics and a remark that Social Statics is 'withdrawn from circulation', no explicit change-of-mind passage. Also Spencer already appears in the existing set (ethics).

lead: Frederick Douglass: Constitution pro-slavery or anti-slavery
reason: The announcement is clear and states the new view (My Bondage and My Freedom 1855, Life and Times 1881: 'I became convinced ... the constitution ... is, in its letter and spirit, an anti-slavery instrument'), but no early Douglass text on Gutenberg states the Garrisonian view in his own words: the Narrative (1845) only carries Garrison's and Phillips's prefaces ('No union with slaveholders') and Douglass's own text has no passage on the Constitution.

lead: Wordsworth: Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff (1793, in Grosart's Prose Works, Gutenberg 16550) vs The Prelude (Books X-XII)
reason: Both are on Gutenberg, but the Prelude's retrospective (e.g. 'the errors into which I fell ... Yielded up moral questions in despair') is verse with line numbers every five lines embedded in the Gutenberg text, so any passage would carry the numerals; and it is a narrative retrospective rather than a plain statement that he changed his mind.

lead: Ruskin: Seven Lamps / Stones of Venice anti-Catholicism vs Praeterita
reason: Praeterita is not on Gutenberg in English; the archive.org OCR gives only a retrospective description of his Protestant zeal (no retraction of a stated thesis), and the 1880 Seven Lamps preface is in the same work as the early passages.

lead: Lead list items not pursued: Coleridge (Biographia vs early Hartleian writings), Southey (Wat Tyler vs Colloquies), A. R. Wallace, Gibbon, Paine, Burke, Comte, Leslie Stephen
reason: Only checked availability: Coleridge's and Southey's early statements are in verse or not on Gutenberg (no Wat Tyler, no prose early text), and I found no documented announced retraction for the others within the budget; stopped after the six verified cases.
